What do the symbols in William Blake's "The Tyger" represent? SYMBOLS IN WILLIAM BLAKE’S “THE TYGER” by Michael R. Burch William Blake’s poem “The Tyger” is laden with symbols and yet is the most anthologized poem in the English language. “The Tyger” has thus been perused and enjoyed by hundreds of millions, if not billions, of readers since it was first published in 1794. How laden with symbols? As I will demonstrate in my analysis, every line of “The Tyger” contains a symbol, and some lines contain multiple symbols. However, these symbols are accessible and easily understood. “The Tyger” is an easy poem to understand, if we connect the dots. However, the majority of readers have failed to connect the dots and thus have entirely missed the poem’s main point, which is wildly heretical and casts extreme doubt on the nature and intentions of God, as I will explain in my analysis of “The Tyger” below. But first, who was William Blake? William Blake was an English poet, painter, engraver and mystic who included “The Tyger” in his 1794 collection Songs of Experience. Ironically, Blake had to self-publish his books because he was considered mad and his poetry of little account. However, readers of the future would judge otherwise and today William Blake is widely acclaimed as one of the world’s greatest and most influential poets. Elsewhere, I have argued that Blake is the world’s most influential poet in terms of his impact on human societies and culture, due to his anti-establishment, reform-minded influence on wildly popular singer-songwriters like Bob Dylan, John Lennon, Jim Morrison, et al. Morrison named his band The Doors after Blake’s “doors of perception.” When the Beatles met Bob Dylan the first time, things were a bit chilly until Allen Ginsberg broke the ice by bringing up the subject of William Blake’s poetry. It turned out that both Dylan and the Fab Four were enthusiastic fans of Blake. Blake has also had tremendous influence on other poets, visual artists, novelists, graphic novelists, cartoonists and filmmakers. And now, without further ado, this is my analysis of “The Tyger” including the poem’s various symbols and “how to connect the dots”… The Tyger by William Blake Tyger Tyger, burning bright, [1] In the forests of the night; [2] What immortal hand or eye, [3] Could frame thy fearful symmetry? [4] [1] Things that are bright are notable and attract our attention. The tiger is a magnificent, stunningly beautiful creature. [2] Forests symbolize nature and like the tiger are both beautiful and dangerous. The night symbolizes darkness, danger and things that are hidden, unseen and mysterious. [3] The “immortal hand” symbolizes the artistry and handiwork of the Creator. Artists like Blake create with their hands. Meanwhile, artists use their eyes to regard and judge their work. The Bible claims God saw his creation, and that in his eyes it was good. Those of us who see a world full of cruelty, suffering and death might argue otherwise, as Blake will in his most famous poem. [4] Here I believe “fearful symmetry” symbolizes seeming perfection in the merger of opposites: in the tiger’s case, extreme beauty with extreme deadliness and cruelty. The tiger is a beautiful but savage predator. Here, we see Blake subtly questioning the nature and intentions of the Creator, but he will be more explicit later. In what distant deeps or skies [5] Burnt the fire of thine eyes? [6] On what wings dare he aspire? [7] What the hand, dare seize the fire? [8] [5] In the opening verses of Genesis, the Creator created the depths [seas] and skies [the visible sky and the heavens above]. The modifier “distant” suggests things beyond the ability of human beings to see or understand. Thus the deeps may symbolize hell and the skies heaven. A critical question in Blake’s poem will be why the Creator fashioned the planet earth as he did, and what his intentions for human beings are. [6] Here fire symbolizes heat, passion, anger and destruction. Fire is also associated with hell and damnation. The Bible refers to a “lake of fire” and its place was said to be deep below the earth. If we combine lines five and six, Blake might be asking whether the tiger was created in heaven or hell. [7] Gods and angels have often been depicted with wings, which thus symbolize both divinity and abilities beyond those of human beings: to fly, to enter heaven, etc. To aspire is to intend and thus symbolizes what Christians call the “divine plan” but which Blake severely doubts, as we will see. [8] Here the hand seizing the fire symbolizes the Gnostic idea that the Creator was “in over his head” and that nothing good would come of his creation. According to gnostic theology, the Creator was evil, not good, and this explains why we live in a world ruled by cruelty, suffering and death. Hands that seize fire get burned, so Blake may be prophesying that the Creator will have to pay for his misdeeds. And what shoulder, & what art, [9] Could twist the sinews of thy heart? [10] And when thy heart began to beat. [11] What dread hand? & what dread feet? [12] [9] Here the art is the method of the art of creation. Was it a dark art? I believe Blake thought so. Sculptors use their shoulders as well as their hands, and here shoulders suggest strength and heavy lifting. [10] Sinews also symbolize strength. The heart symbolizes courage. The tiger is wonderfully courageous and has a mighty heart, but how is that mighty heart employed? [11] The heart beginning to beat symbolizes the moment of birth, of creation. But what happens when that mighty heart begins to beat? Savagery, destruction, death. [12] The dread hand and dread feet are those of the Creator. Is the Creator even more savage and dreadful than his fearsome creation, the tiger? What the hammer? what the chain, [13] In what furnace was thy brain? [14] What the anvil? what dread grasp [15] Dare its deadly terrors clasp? [16] [13] The hammer symbolizes the creative powers of the Creator, but he is hammering out a chain on his anvil of creation. In another poem Blake railed against the “mind-forg’d manacles” that keep human beings slaves of church [bad religion] and state [bad government] and their own bad thinking. Here it seems this chaining, this enslavement, was part and parcel of creation. According to the Genesis creation account, Adam and Eve were created to be gardeners in an animal state, lacking the knowledge of good and evil. Was this the intention of the Creator? Blake seems to think so. [14] Here the furnace may symbolize hell. Was the tiger’s savage brain forged in hell rather than in heaven? [15] The anvil symbolizes where creation takes place. A blacksmith’s anvil is surrounded by fire, sparks and smoke. Is this a hellish anvil? Yes, it seems obviously so. The “dread grasp” echoes previous characteristics of the Creator. Is he more dreadful than his most dreadful creation, the tiger? [16] The “dread grasp” clasping “deadly terrors” again symbolizes and questions the nature of the Creator. What sort of Being is able to dominate the savage tiger while fashioning chains to enslave it? And what are this Being’s intentions for human beings? When the stars threw down their spears [17] And water'd heaven with their tears: [18] Did he smile his work to see? [19] Did he who made the Lamb make thee? [20] [17] To the ancients the stars were divine beings — gods, angels, great hunters and heroes of yore who had become immortal after death. Does the throwing down of spears symbolize acknowledgement that the Creator was the greatest of them all? Or did the other divine beings throw down their spears in disgust? [18] Here, the stars watering heaven with their tears strongly suggests the other divine beings were very unhappy with the Creator’s handiwork. Why? Because they understood what the creation of the tiger meant for all the other creatures, and for human beings. [19] The Bible says the Creator saw his work as good, hence this smile symbolizes the happiness of the Creator with his creation, and with the tiger, the ultimate predator. [20] Here the Lamb is capitalized, and this is no accident. The lamb symbolizes innocence and purity with its downy coat of white wool, vulnerability, sacrifice, and the person of Jesus Christ, who was called the Lamb of God. Furthermore, the Lamb capitalized refers to Blake’s poem “The Lamb” which appeared in Songs of Innocence and is a companion poem to “The Tyger.” When Blake asks, “Did he who made the Lamb make thee?” he is asking a freighted question for Christians and for everyone who claims that “God is good.” Blake is questioning the nature of a God who would create an innocent, defenseless lamb to be ripped to shreds and eaten by such a savage predator as the tiger. And he is questioning the nature of a God who would send his “only begotten son” to earth to be crucified as a bloody sacrifice. Elsewhere, Blake would call this alleged god NOBODADDY because no one would want him for a father. Tyger Tyger burning bright, In the forests of the night: What immortal hand or eye, Dare frame thy fearful symmetry? Blake ends his famous poem the way he began it, with the exception of the word “dare” in the concluding line. Is Blake asking, “How dare the Creator do what he did, and will he pay for his crimes against life?” At least that’s the way I interpret the poem. by Michael R. Burch The legend of what happened "on a dark and stormy" night at Tintagel is endlessly intriguing. Supposedly, Merlin transformed Uther Pendragon to look like Gorlois so that Uther could sleep with Ygraine, the lovely wife of the unlucky duke. While Uther was enjoying Ygraine’s lovemaking, Gorlois was off getting himself killed. Did Igraine suspect that her lover was not her husband? In any case, Artur/Artos/Arthur was the child conceived out of this supernatural (?) encounter. That night, at Tintagel, there was darkness such as man had never seen ... darkness and treachery, and the unholy thundering of the sea ... In his arms, who can say how much she knew? And if he whispered her name ... “Ygraine!” ... could she tell above the howling wind and rain? Could she tell, or did she care, by the length of his hair or the heat of his flesh, ... that her faceless companion was Uther, the dragon, and Gorlois lay dead? I've long felt that I owe much of my success as a poet to Merlyn & Co., because my career didn't really take off until I became inspired to write about the "real" Arthur of the ancient Celtic myths. I found no joy in that addled boy, nor he at my breast. Why him? Why him? As the candles dim, it grows harder and harder to say ... Perhaps girls and boys are the god’s toys when they lose their way. Originally published by Celtic Twilight as "The First Time" Isolde’s Song by Michael R. Burch According to legend, Isolde and Tristram/Tristan were lovers who died, were buried close to each other, then reunited in the form of plants growing out of their graves. There was relief there, without remorse when the tin whistle lifted its voice in a tune of artless grief, piping achingly high and longingly of an island veiled in myth. And the Celtic cross that stands here tells us, not of their grief, but of their faith and belief— like the last soft breath of evening lifting a fallen leaf. When ravenous famine set all her demons loose, driving men to the seas like lemmings, they sought here the clemency of a better life, or death, and their belief in God gave them hope, a sense of peace. These were proud men with only their lives to owe, who sought the liberation of a strange new land. Now they lie here, ragged row on ragged row, with only the shadows of their loved ones close at hand. According to legend, Cædmon, an illiterate Anglo-Saxon cowherd, received the gift of poetic composition from an angel; he subsequently founded a school of Christian poets. Unfortunately, only nine lines of Cædmon’s verse survive, in the writings of the Venerable Bede. Whitby, tiny as it is, reappears later in the history of English literature, having been visited, in diametric contrast, by Lewis Carroll and Bram Stoker’s ghoulish yet evocative Dracula. At the monastery of Whitby, on a day when the sun sank through the sea, and the gulls shrieked wildly, jubilant, free, while the wind and time blew all around, I paced those dusk-enamored grounds and thought I heard the steps resound of Carroll, Stoker and good Bede who walked there, too, their spirits freed —perhaps by God, perhaps by need— to write, and with each line, remember the glorious light of Cædmon’s ember, scorched tongues of flame words still engender. Here, as darkness falls, at last we meet. I lay this pale garland of words at his feet. Originally published by The Lyric
